item.title: Paraguay Senate impeaches President Peña, VP Alliana takes over
item.description: Pedro Alliana became president of Paraguay on Friday following the impeachment of his predecessor over a massive banking crisis that locked almost half the country out of their accounts. Senators appointed Alliana, the former vice president, shortly after voting to remove Santiago Pena over the chaotic collapse of a bank to which he had links. Senate President Basilio Nunez declared Pena “guilty of poor performance in his duties” after 44 out of 45 senators voted in favor of impeachment, with one lawmaker absent. Hundreds of people waiting outside Congress raucously celebrated his impeachment. “Justice has been done. Now we want him to give us back our money and go to jail,” Jessica Aquino, 32, told AFP. Paraguayan authorities placed the ex-leader under house arrest minutes after his removal, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester told reporters. Alliana promised not to abandon the almost three million depositors, including pensioners, affected by Ueno Bank’s takeover amid insolvency concerns. “Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated,” said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028. Opposition lawmakers had also filed a motion to impeach Alliana over the crisis, but the request failed to gain congressional approval. – Money trickles back – The bank’s demise brought thousands of people onto the streets demanding repercussions for US-backed Pena, who until last year had a stake in Grupo Vazquez, which controlled Ueno. Advance payments to an unspecified number of impacted depositors began on Thursday afternoon, a Central Bank official told AFP. The first phase of aid deposits, up to around $1,600, will go to clients who don’t have loans and have an account at another bank or institution in Paraguay to receive the funds, said Jose Maciel of the Central Bank’s Deposit Guarantee Fund. The next beneficiaries “will be announced progressively over the course of the payment process,” he added. Pena had offered his resignation over the disaster, but lawmakers pressed ahead with impeachment proceedings that have stripped him of political immunity. The opposition accused the US-backed politician of a conflict of interest, which he denied. The Attorney General said it was investigating him for “acts related to the supervision and resolution of Ueno Bank S.A. and the placement of public funds in said entity.” He will be questioned over alleged crimes of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds on Saturday, prosecutor Gonzalez Vester said. Pena urged reconciliation in an X post shortly before his removal. “Today, we must come together as Paraguayans to rebuild our institutions and restore trust,” he said. item.title: Houston mayor limits immigration agents cooperation by police after Democratic victory
item.description: The mayor of Houston, Texas announced Friday that the city’s police department will limit its cooperation with federal immigration agents after Democrats swept midterm elections this week. The so-called “blue tsunami” ousted Republican Governor Greg Abbott, a close Texas ally of US President Donald Trump, who has cracked down on immigration with raids conducted by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents since returning to office last year. Abbott had threatened in April to revoke $110 million in public safety funding from Houston if city officials didn’t walk back a similar measure earlier this year, and city officials complied. He lost reelection on Tuesday and will be replaced by Democrat Gina Hinojosa, the first Latina woman elected governor of Texas. Now, Houston Mayor John Whitmire has signed an executive order instructing Houston police to not contact ICE agents when a person is detained for nonviolent offenses, like a traffic stop. “It’s to reduce the fear and anxiety, not just in some of our communities but across Houston,” Whitmire said during a press conference announcing the change. The 77-year-old mayor acknowledged that the change could bring some political risks but said he was ready to meet them, as Abbott and other Republicans remain in power until January. ICE released a statement on X reacting to the change, writing: “Watching child porn and selling heroin are classified as ‘nonviolent offenses’ by the way.” “This is the Mayor of Houston directly advocating for policies that protect some of the worst criminals in America,” it added. According to the Prison Policy Initiative, a nonpartisan think tank, Texas has had more arrests carried out by ICE agents during Trump’s second term than any other state, with almost 137,000 recorded as of August 2026. Texas is also the state with the highest number of ICE detainees in the US, with over 16,000 held at various facilities — more than double the amount held in the second highest state, Louisiana — according to Syracuse University’s Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse. item.title: How pregnant woman delivered inside Danfo in Lagos
item.description: By Olasunkanmi Akoni Passengers inside a commercial bus, popularly called Danfo in Lagos were stunned when a fellow passenger suddenly went into sudden labor and successfully gave birth to a baby boy on board. According to Lagos State Emergency Management Agency, LASEMA, the woman was traveling across the state when labor began unexpectedly mid-journey In the process, fellow commuters and onlookers quickly assisted her through the delivery inside the vehicle while others went into prayer session for safe delivery. Medical responders and local commuters assisted in securing the mother and child immediately following the emergency delivery. Fortunately, after few minutes, the baby boy was delivered safely. In viral footage capturing the moments following the birth, witnesses suggested naming the child Abiona—a traditional Yoruba name commonly associated with a child born on a journey or along the road. Recall that a similar incident happened at Onipanu Bus Stop, along Ikorodu Road sometimes ago. “In a swift r​esponse, LASEMA arrived at the scene to assist a pregnant woman who went into sudden labor while waiting for transport. “The woman delivered a healthy baby boy. Both mother and child were stabilized by LASEMA paramedics before being transported to a nearby healthcare facility for post-natal care,” LASEMA Permanent Secretary, Dr. Femi Oke-Osanyintolu stated. item.title: The Records Are On The Ballot
item.description: The campaign has acquired a sharper edge: In Akwa Ibom Today, President Bola Tinubu challenged the leadership credentials of his principal opponents. His apparent references to Peter Obi’s handling of erosion in Anambra and Atiku Abubakar’s departure from the PDP sought to turn their past decisions into questions about their fitness to govern. These were campaign accusations, rather than independently established assessments of their records. Vice-President Kashim Shettima reinforced the attack, questioning Obi’s credibility and arguing that Atiku’s experience should be judged by accomplishments rather than years in office. His assertion that Obi has lost goodwill remains a partisan assessment; it does not establish a measurable change in voter support. The political intention is clear: put the challengers on the defensive. That matters for an incumbent whose own performance is under examination. If voters spend more time debating whether the opposition is credible, the government gains room to argue that continuity is the safer choice. But scrutiny travels both ways. Once the campaign becomes a comparison of records, Tinubu must also answer for the results of his presidency: purchasing power, security, employment and public services. UYO: Projects and Political Persuasion Today’s visit combined the inauguration of projects executed by Governor Umo Eno’s administration with a political gathering. It gave Tinubu a setting in which visible infrastructure and electoral advocacy could reinforce each other. The distinction between state projects and federal achievements still matters. Political cooperation can support delivery, but credit should follow the evidence about funding, execution and responsibility. For the governing camp, the opportunity is to connect infrastructure with an argument about competent government. For voters, the question is how those investments improve transport, commerce, services and livelihoods. An inauguration provides a powerful picture. Its electoral value depends on the public’s experience after the ceremony. ATIKU: Defiance Needs a Legal Foundation Atiku’s response today remained combative. In a statement, he accused the government of using the courts to evade electoral judgment and reaffirmed his intention to challenge the ruling. That allegation requires attribution; it is not proof of government direction of the proceedings. His campaign also continued in Kebbi on Thursday, despite the judgment. Reporting published today describes promises on security, employment and restoring fuel subsidies. The event should therefore be treated as yesterday’s campaign activity, rather than a fresh Friday rally. Politically, continuing to campaign signals resolve. item.title: Nigeria Presides Over Key UN Election
item.description: Nigeria has presided over key elections at the United Nations General Assembly’s Fifth Committee, with Mauritania and Israel emerging as beneficiaries of two significant appointments during the 81st Session of the General Assembly. The elections, conducted under the chairmanship of Nigeria’s permanent representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Jimoh Ibrahim, saw C.D. Mohammed of Mauritania recommended as Chair of the International Civil Service Commission, while Israel’s candidate, Shai Mazai, secured a place on the Independent Audit Advisory Committee. In a demonstration of transparency in the electoral process, Ambassador Ibrahim directed that the ballot boxes be opened before voting commenced, allowing delegates to verify the boxes ahead of the collection of ballots. In the contest for the chairmanship of the International Civil Service Commission, C.D. Mohammed of Mauritania secured 102 votes, defeating Mrs. Maria of Zimbabwe, who polled 82 votes. Having obtained the required majority of 93 votes, Mohammed was recommended by the Fifth Committee to the General Assembly for designation as Chair of the International Civil Service Commission for a four-year term beginning January 1, 2027. In another significant outcome, Israel’s Mr. Shai Mazai secured 134 votes to emerge as the recommended candidate from the Group of Western European and Other States to the Independent Audit Advisory Committee. The Fifth Committee subsequently recommended his appointment to the committee for a three-year term, also beginning January 1, 2027. The elections formed part of the Committee’s consideration of Agenda Item 119, which covers appointments to fill vacancies in subsidiary organs and other appointments. Other bodies considered during the exercise included the Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions, the Committee on Contributions and the Investment Committee, alongside the International Civil Service Commission and the Independent Audit Advisory Committee. The Fifth Committee, chaired by Ambassador Jimoh Ibrahim, also recommended candidates from other regional groups to the International Civil Service Commission through acclamation, following the absence of contested nominations for the respective seats. At the conclusion of the exercise, Ambassador Ibrahim commended delegates for their patience, cooperation and commitment throughout the electoral process. He also congratulated those recommended for appointment and urged them to uphold the integrity of the Fifth Committee while discharging their responsibilities. The Nigerian diplomat equally acknowledged the contributions of the tellers and officials nominated by Member States to supervise the electoral process. Ambassador Ibrahim subsequently declared the Committee’s consideration of Agenda Item 119 concluded and requested the Rapporteur to communicate its decisions to the General Assembly for further action. item.title: 2027: Opposition’s battle for space
item.description: Within a span of one week, opposition political parties in Nigeria have experienced various challenges in their bid to contest in the 2027 general elections. From the bids for the presidency to governorship, national assembly and state assembly seats, opposition candidates have not been finding it easy to campaign as they wish as they are faced with various forms of harassment, suppression and intimidation. Weekend Trust reports that 31 states in the country are under the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) while two of the remaining five opposition governors have been included in the presidential campaign council of the party. Our correspondents recall that within the week, the convoy of the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) was attacked in Cross Rivers State, while the bid by the African Democratic Congress (ADC) to hold a rally in Sokoto met with stiff opposition and in Edo and Plateau States, the billboards of major opposition candidates were pulled down. Habiba: The woman behind ‘Jaiz Bank’s N100m investment scheme’ The night of January 15, 1966 – General Paul Tarfa On Thursday, a Federal High Court sitting in Abuja also nullified all the processes of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) that led to the emergence of former Vice President Atiku Abubakar as the party’s candidate for the 2027 election. Justice Peter Lifu, in a judgement, nullified the emergence of the former Senate President, David Mark, Rauf Aregbesola and others as national officers of the ADC. The judge held that the nominations of candidates for the 2027 general elections were cancelled on account of emerging from an “illegal and unlawful leadership.” In the same day, the presidential campaign convoy of the ADC was reportedly attacked in Kebbi State, as the candidate, Atiku, moved through Kebbi on campaign engagements on Thursday. According to reports from the campaign team, thugs blocked the convoy and pelted vehicles with stones. These developments, according to political observers, represent a systematic weakening of opposition parties and raise concerns over Nigeria’s democracy. Due to the frequency in occurrence, opposition figures and civil society organisations have accused the ruling party, APC, of utilizing state-backed coercion, judicial manipulation, and targeted inducements to systematically dismantle counter-balancing political structures across the country. Critics warn that by neutralising alternative political platforms ahead of upcoming electoral cycles, the APC-led administration is actively eroding the essential checks and balances required for democratic accountability. item.title: Habiba: The woman behind ‘Jaiz Bank’s N100m investment scheme’
item.description: The protest over the N104 million Mudarabah investment and the alleged withdrawal from customers’ accounts at Jaiz Bank, Jos, on Monday, has raised questions with many asking how such could have occurred. One staff member of the bank, Habiba Abdulrahman, is at the centre of the scandal. Mrs Abdulrahman, 35, is a resident of Muhammadu Wada Street, Jos North Local Government Area of Plateau State. She had her primary education at Women Association Primary School, Jos. Thereafter, she proceeded to Federal Government Girls’ College, Bauchi. In 2009, she gained admission into the Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University (ATBU), Bauchi, where she read Environmental Management Technology. She taught at Esteem Secondary School. And between 2018 and 2019, she was employed by Jaiz Bank as a contract customer service officer and subsequently rose to the position of Operations Head (Backup), with the primary duty of approving withdrawals and transfers initiated by tellers in the bank. 2027: Opposition’s battle for space The night of January 15, 1966 – General Paul Tarfa Weekend Trust gathered that Habiba was sacked by the bank in January 2026, after the irregularities were detected. On Monday this week, affected customers who found their accounts emptied by the alleged sacked staff staged a protest in front of the bank in Jos, asking it to refund their money. They also called on the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) and other relevant authorities to come to their aid, adding that despite several complaints to the bank’s management, the money had not been refunded. The customers alleged that when the matter was earlier reported to the bank’s management, they were informed that the money had been transferred to several bank accounts by a staff member. The protesters insisted that the transactions were carried out within the banking hall using documents approved by the bank. The protesters at the entrance of the bank on Monday. We found fake Jaiz Bank certificates of fixed deposits, documents in Habiba’s house – Police Following a complaint to the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) of the Plateau State police command by the Jaiz Bank Jos branch manager, Victoria Amidu, in January this year, the CID arrested Habiba, Weekend Trust gathered. In its findings dated June 19, 2026, obtained by Weekend Trust from the lawyer of one of the victims, N. A. Idoko, the CID accused Habiba of conspiracy, cheating and fraud during her transactions with the affected customers. The police also accused Habiba of conniving with her husband, Manir Murtala, 44, and her younger sister, Zainab Abdulrahman, 21, whose accounts were allegedly used to transfer customers’ money into theirs. item.title: The night of January 15, 1966 – General Paul Tarfa
item.description: General Paul Chabiri Tarfa joined the Nigerian Army as a cadet in 1962 and remained there until 1988, serving for 26 years. In that span of time he held many positions – Assistant Adjutant General, Provost Marshal, Commandant of the Nigerian Defence Academy. He also served as the governor of the old Oyo State in 1978. After retirement, he served as the managing director of the Nigerian Railways and also had a brief assignment to reorganise the Nigerian Customs. At 85, he is still busy as the chairman of the North-East Development Commission. He shared his experiences with Weekend Trust. I would like to start with your home, Garkida, which I think is a well-known centre for missionary and western education. Do you think the fact that you were born there has had a very huge impact on how your life turned out? Of course, Garkida is one of the old places in the North where missionaries set up and gave us good footing in education. I must say that in those days we were privileged to have been among the early people in the North, especially the North-East, to be introduced to western education. Habiba: The woman behind ‘Jaiz Bank’s N100m investment scheme’ 2027: Opposition’s battle for space That is not to say that Islamic education was not there, but surely, we were lucky to have the missionaries as far back as March 1923, to be precise. You can imagine that it is well over 100 years now. We have benefitted. We had early education and were introduced to secondary school. We had good medical care, which many of our people in the North were not privileged to have. We went from primary to secondary school, from where we had the advantage of being successfully qualified to get enrolled into the Nigerian Army. I think you went to secondary school in Yola and not Garkida, right? Well, Garkida laid the foundation before going to Yola – provincial secondary school in those days. There were only 12 in the entire North and Yola was one of them. It was from there that I had the opportunity to get into the army. You became a cadet in the army in April 1962, but it didn’t take long before you were taken to Canada, a very strange place for someone coming from this part of the world. Before going there, we were told what it would be. Even before then, in Geography in secondary school, we had known about temperate countries, hot countries and so on, of which Canada was one. So when we got to Canada, we were very well equipped and properly prepared, physically and mentally. Your career in the army took off after you returned to Canada. This was 1963? Yes. We came back in December 1963, received at Kano airport, taken to Kaduna and received by the duty officer, who at that time happened to be a man called Benjamin Adekunle. item.title: Anambra will deliver over 50% of 2027 votes to Tinubu — Soludo
item.description: By Vincent Ujumadu Anambra State Governor, Prof. Chukwuma Soludo, has promised to deliver at least 50 percent of the state’s votes to President Bola Tinubu, the presidential candidate of the All Progressives Congress (APC), in the 2027 general elections. Read Also: Tinubu to Nigerians: ‘I promise better future’ The governor made the declaration during the flag off of the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA) 2027 campaign at Ekwueme Square, Awka. According to him, APGA has no presidential candidate for the 2027 general election and would, therefore, adopt President Tinubu as its preferred candidate. “Today, we adopt the APC presidential candidate, Bola Ahmed Tinubu as our candidate,” he declared, noting that the president had demonstrated love and concern for the Igbo people, particularly the people of Anambra State. The governor recalled that the President had appointed several Anambra indigenes to strategic positions in Lagos State during his tenure as governor. He also recalled that APGA had adopted the presidential candidate of the ruling party in previous elections, noting that the party’s decision to support Tinubu in 2027 was a continuation of that political arrangement that had been in existence. He lamented that Anambra State recorded fewer than 5,000 votes for Tinubu in the 2023 presidential election, yet the President has continued to address some of the challenges confronting the state and the South-East region. He urged the Anambra electorate to support Tinubu in the 2027 election, arguing that doing so would give the state and the South-East a stronger opportunity to engage with the Federal Government and negotiate for their development. “We need to vote for him in order to sit with the government at the centre and negotiate for the development of the South-East and Anambra State”, he declared. item.title: Tinubu’s reforms need time to deliver, 2nd term will consolidate gains — Aguda
item.description: Oluwole Aguda is a businessman, consultant on electoral mat- ters and political affairs, and a former governorship aspirant in Kogi State, under the African Action Con- gress (AAC) in 2019. In this interview, he examines President Bola Tinubu’s reform agenda, the steps the President must take to secure electoral support in the North ahead of the 2027 general election, and the political implications of the lingering face-off between Imo State Governor Hope Uzodimma and his predecessor, Senator Rochas Okoro- cha, over the Imo West senatorial ticket. Excerpts: Given the hardship caused by fuel subsidy removal, naira devaluation and other economic policies, what tangible improvements in Nigerians’ living conditions can President Tinubu point to as justification for seeking a second term? A fair assessment requires us to examine the immediate challenges confronting the economy and the long-term benefits expected from the reforms. Nigeria’s economy was bleeding, and stopping that haemorrhage was necessary to give the country a chance of recovery. Ending fuel subsidy addressed an avenue for corruption and the unsustainable drain on public resources. NELFUND had disbursed over N300 billion to over 1.5m students across 319 tertiary institutions as at October 2026. However, I would not suggest that these developments have largely translated into improved living conditions for most Nigerians. That remains the administration’s biggest challenge. The cost of food, transportation, housing, healthcare and other essentials continues to put enormous pressure on households. Economic recovery must ultimately be measured by whether people can afford necessities, businesses can employ more workers and incomes can support a reasonable standard of living. The President’s case for another term should not rest solely on the courage to introduce reforms. It must also depend on translating them into better purchasing power, employment, productivity and social welfare. Reforms require time, but Nigerians enduring difficult adjustments must see a credible pathway to relief. How would you assess the Tinubu administration’s performance, and what justifies giving it another four years? There is intention coupled with execution across different sectoral interventions. While execution has been a challenge, progressive steps have been made. Investment in our military is important to sustaining a motivated Army, Navy and Air Force in the war against terrorism. item.title: US offers $20m reward for info on ‘Iran’s nuclear program’: CENTCOM
item.description: Washington is offering a $20 million reward “and possible relocation” for information about Iran’s nuclear program, the US military said Friday, as President Donald Trump reiterated Tehran wants to make a deal to end the war. Read Also: Iran warns of wider war if US attacks after Trump election rout A State Department program, Rewards for Justice, “is offering a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community,” US Central Command said on X. The program was established in 1984 under the State Department’s national security rewards program to offer money for information that protects American lives and interests. In its statement about the reward, the State Department said Iran’s “lack of compliance with the IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency) on safeguards obligations has led to the agency’s loss of ‘continuity of knowledge’ regarding Iran’s production and inventory of key components like centrifuges. It gave no specific parameters on what information would yield a $20 million reward. Trump has repeatedly said US forces have effectively obliterated Iran’s nuclear program. “If we didn’t hit Iran, you wouldn’t have Israel today,” Trump said Friday night in West Palm Beach, Florida. “If they had nuclear, they would have used nuclear. They would have obliterated the Middle East.” But the president also said Iran – which he stressed has had its economy and military severely damaged over eight months of war – is eager to end the conflict. “We’re dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly,” he said. Diplomatic efforts by mediators have been in full swing in an attempt to prevent any resumption of fighting. And on Tuesday Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said his government was still trying to resolve the crisis through dialogue. Earlier this week Trump said he still had to “take care” of one or two targets, including so-called Pickaxe Mountain in central Iran, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility. item.title: Trump: Lesson for Nigeria, by Stephanie Shaakaa
item.description: Donald Trump wanted the November 3 midterm elections to be about him. He said so repeatedly, urging Americans to vote as though his name were on the ballot. He wanted a Republican victory to demonstrate that his presidency still commanded popular support and that his influence over American politics remained firmly intact. Well, Americans took him seriously. Perhaps more seriously than he expected. Democrats have won control of both chambers of the United States Congress, delivering a major electoral setback to Trump and his Republican Party. Yet, as the results became clear, Trump reached for an explanation that seemed to contradict his own campaign message. In a post on his Truth Social platform, he declared: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” The irony is difficult to miss. He had spent weeks asking Americans to treat the election as a verdict on his presidency. When the verdict went against him, he suddenly appeared to be distancing himself from it. He wanted the political benefits of making the election about him without accepting the consequences when voters delivered an unfavourable answer. For readers in Nigeria, it is worth explaining what America calls midterm elections and why they matter. In the United States, a president is elected for a four-year term, but congressional elections take place every two years. This means that halfway into a president’s tenure, Americans return to the polls to elect members of the legislature. These elections are called midterms because they take place in the middle of a presidential term. Congress has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate. All 435 seats in the House are contested every two years, while senators serve six-year terms, with approximately one-third of the 100 Senate seats contested every two years. Midterm elections do not determine who becomes president. The sitting president remains in office. Instead, voters decide which party controls Congress and, by extension, how much support or opposition the president will face in the legislature This gives Americans an opportunity to express satisfaction or dissatisfaction with a president’s performance without waiting another four years. They can strengthen the president’s party in Congress or hand control to the opposition, making it considerably more difficult for the president to advance his legislative agenda. That is precisely what has happened to Trump. American presidents often benefit from what is known as the coattail effect. When a president is popular, candidates from the same party can benefit from that popularity. His political strength becomes an advantage for others seeking elective office. But when a president becomes unpopular, the effect can work in reverse. Candidates associated with his administration may find themselves paying the price for public dissatisfaction with his leadership. item.title: From open pavilion to nation of orderlies: Is Zik’s ‘fear-free’ Nigeria still possible?
item.description: .What a 1960 inauguration says about fear in today’s corridors of power By Omeiza Ajayi Nearly 66 years after Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe was sworn in as Nigeria’s first African Governor-General, the footage of that day – which has again recently gone viral – raises an uncomfortable question: why did a leader who held the highest office in the land need no retinue of security details standing behind him, while today every minister, and even some local government supervisors, cannot move without a swarm of details? The inauguration took place on November 16, 1960, at Tafawa Balewa Square, barely six weeks after independence. It was also Zik’s 56th birthday. The narrator of the newsreel set the scene plainly. “At the steps of the pavilion stand the Prime Minister and the Lord Chief Justice, symbolising the people and the law, on what is surely one of the most important occasions in the history of the country.” No armed escort looms in the frame. No aide hovers at the shoulder of the man the crowd was chanting for. “Zik! Zik!” rang around the square as he arrived, and the vast stands, in the narrator’s words, were “hushed.” Today the picture is reversed. In Abuja and in the state capitals, orderlies trail ministers into halls and offices. The situation is so bad that some security personnel actually enter into very enclosed spaces or rooms with their AK47 rifles in clear breach of security protocol. At the local government level, some unelected supervisory councillors have been known to move with armed vigilance team members or hunters, sometimes to intimidate the very people they were appointed to serve. The easy explanation is insecurity, and it is not a false flag. Banditry, kidnapping and insurgency have made parts of the country dangerous, and no leader can be faulted for fearing for his life. But the leaders of other nations also face threats. Behind the American president or a British prime minister stand trained protective officers, assigned to a defined danger. They do not crowd every public official, from the cabinet room to the ward office, with men whose chief duty is to announce importance. It is not uncommon in Nigeria to see security details standing and blocking a television camera. That leaves the harder question. Are Nigeria’s leaders afraid of the general state of the country, or have they become afraid of their own people? Zik, standing in the open that November morning, appeared to have settled that question for himself. He began his address with these words: “It is with humility, mingled with joy, that I thank this grand concourse of patriots and friends of Nigeria for congregating here today on the occasion of my inauguration as the first African Governor General and Commander-in-Chief of the Federation of Nigeria.” He titled the speech “Respect for Human Dignity,” and he made no secret of what he feared for Nigeria. item.description: By Clifford Ndujihe & Benjamin Njoku Chief John Odafe Asiemo, 57, popularly known as Daddy Showkey, is a household name in Nigerian music scene. I remember saying one day while walking past Vanguard ‘this newspaper will one day write about me.’ It came to pass when Ogbonnaya wrote about me for the first time. The second was Smart Irewudo, a former Champion Newspaper reporter, now based in the United States. Before I started recording, during the June 12 crisis, I led Ajegunle boys who blocked roads and extorted money from motorists. Smart took my picture and published it in the Daily Champion. item.title: Police rescue 10 stolen children in Abia
item.description: By Steve Oko UMUAHIA—The Abia State Police Command has arrested suspects linked to the October 17 attack on Uratta Divisional Police Headquarters, rescued 10 stolen children and recovered 15 firearms and 30 stolen vehicles in a major security crackdown across the state. The Command also disclosed that it arrested 109 suspects, comprising 89 males and 20 females, in connection with 211 criminal cases recorded between September 11, 2026 and November 6, 2026. Commissioner of Police, CP Wilfred Afolabi, who disclosed this on Friday while presenting the Command’s operational scorecard, said the arrests followed intelligence-driven operations and collaboration with other security agencies. On the Uratta police station attack, Afolabi said investigations had led to the arrest of some of the suspected attackers, with one of them allegedly confessing to leading the gang that carried out the assault. He said investigations were ongoing to track down other accomplices and establish the full circumstances surrounding the attack. In a related security operation, operatives of the Anti-Kidnapping Unit raided a location at Ubakala, Umuahia South Local Government Area, on October 25, arresting a suspect identified as Osita. The police reportedly recovered two locally fabricated guns, 16 live cartridges and four expended cartridges from the suspect. Another suspect, 30-year-old suspect, was subsequently arrested for allegedly supplying ammunition illegally. Both suspects have been charged to court, according to the CP. On child trafficking, Afolabi said police operatives rescued 10 children during the period under review and reunited them with their families. He specifically disclosed that two suspects, including a 38-year-old , were arrested on October 11 over the alleged stealing of two children, seven-year-old Chiamaka Chikeze and nine-month-old Goodluck Chikeze. The children were reportedly recovered and handed back to their parents, while the suspects were charged to court. The police boss also announced the arrest of a five-man vehicle theft syndicate, aged 43, and 40. A Toyota Corolla with registration number ROU 9338J was recovered from the suspects, who have also been charged to court. In another operation, two suspected cultists, aged 27, and 25, were arrested on October 31 for allegedly dispossessing students of Abia State University, Uturu, of their mobile phones and other valuables at gunpoint. A locally fabricated firearm was recovered from them. The CP said one of the suspects had confessed to belonging to the Black Axe Confraternity, adding that efforts were ongoing to apprehend other members of the gang. item.title: ‘Sort out your internal mess’, APC tells Atiku, ADC after court judgment
item.description: By Omeiza Ajayi The All Progressives Congress APC has told the Senator David Mark-led faction of the African Democratic Congress ADC to go sort out its internal mess and quit its “senseless rants” after a Federal High Court judgment sacked the faction’s leadership. Read Also: ADC Crisis: What becomes of Atiku, Mark, Gombe if Supreme Court decides party’s fate? In a statement Friday in Abuja, the APC National Publicity Secretary, Felix Morka, said the ruling party had no hand in the case. “To be clear, APC is neither a party nor an interlocutor in the matter. Nothing about the case has anything to do with the APC. And the APC has absolutely no role in the party’s judicial quagmire,” he said. The judgment, delivered on Thursday by Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court, Abuja, sacked the David Mark-led leadership of the ADC. It also nullified all official acts of that leadership, including its primary election processes and outcomes, like the presidential candidacy of former vice president Atiku Abubakar. Morka said the case was brought by ADC national officers against the faction now removed from office, describing the suit as “a notorious case initiated by leaders of ADC against pirate leaders of ADC.” He accused Mark and his associates of taking over the party “to satisfy Atiku Abubakar’s quixotic presidential ambition.” According to him, “it didn’t matter to them that their hostile takeover of that party was in flagrant violation of the rule of law and ADC’s internal democracy, as a court of competent jurisdiction has now declared.” The APC spokesman also accused the ADC of reacting to court decisions according to whether they favour it. “Every time a court decides against the Senator David Mark-led factional African Democratic Congress, they accuse the All Progressives Congress of collusion and deprecate the judiciary. Every time a court decides in their favour, they hail the rule of law and extol the judiciary,” he said. He added that the faction’s attitude showed “no iota of regard for the authority and independence of the judiciary, an indispensable pillar of any democracy.” On Thursday’s ruling, Morka said it “was procured by their own lawlessness and demonstrates the vibrancy of the rule of law and independence of the judiciary in Nigeria.” He said the ADC leaders “take no responsibility or accountability for the self-inflicted injury that the court only judicially certified.” Vanguard News The post ‘Sort out your internal mess’, APC tells Atiku, ADC after court judgment appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Scientists turn cancer cells into weapons against tumours
item.description: By Sola Ogundipe What if the chemical produced in abundance by cancer cells could be turned against the cancers? What if, instead of flooding the entire body with powerful drugs in an attempt to destroy a tumour, scientists could persuade cancer cells to manufacture destructive chemicals from within? That possibility is at the centre of an intriguing scientific breakthrough in Japan, where researchers have developed an experimental technique that exploits carbon monoxide produced by cancer cells to generate cancer-killing compounds inside them. The approach turns an unusual feature of cancer biology into a potential therapeutic advantage. Rather than administering an already manufactured toxic drug that circulates through the body and can damage healthy tissues, the researchers have devised a chemical system that produces an anticancer compound inside targeted cancer cells. In laboratory experiments, the technique successfully generated toxic compounds in several cancer cell lines while leaving a noncancerous cell line without detectable production of the same compound. Although still at an early experimental stage, the findings could open a new direction in cancer treatment, particularly in the long-standing search for ways to destroy malignant cells while sparing healthy tissues from the collateral damage associated with conventional chemotherapy. The research, led by Katsunori Tanaka at the RIKEN Pioneering Research Institute (PRI), Japan, was published in Nature Communications. Cancer treatment has long been complicated by a fundamental problem: drugs powerful enough to destroy malignant cells can also injure normal cells. Chemotherapy, for instance, often affects healthy tissues because many anticancer medicines cannot distinguish perfectly between cancerous and noncancerous cells. The resulting damage can produce debilitating side effects, including nausea, fatigue, hair loss and suppression of the immune system. Scientists have consequently been exploring more selective ways of delivering or generating anticancer agents at the precise location where they are needed. Tanaka and colleagues focused on carbon monoxide, a gas commonly recognised for its toxicity but also naturally produced in small quantities in the human body. Their strategy was to deliver a metal-based catalyst into cells and use the available carbon monoxide as the chemical fuel for a reaction that manufactures an anticancer substance. In principle, the reaction would be activated predominantly in cancer cells, where sufficient carbon monoxide is available, rather than in healthy tissues. The research represents part of a developing scientific field known as therapeutic in vivo synthetic chemistry, which seeks to use chemical reactions inside living organisms to manufacture therapeutic substances where they are needed. item.title: Nigeria is losing $1.6bn yearly to avoidable blindness — Aghaji
item.description: By Prisca Sam-Duru Almost on a daily basis, across Nigeria and much of Africa, millions of people wake up to a world they cannot see clearly. A farmer peeks at his cassava farms for instance, but cannot differentiate the difference between weed and crop. A trader holds her register at arm’s length, guessing at figures she once read at a glance. A child in the back row of a classroom copies from a board that is almost a blur. More often, an old woman needs her grandchild to lead her to the market because the road she walked for over 50 years has become unrecognizable. Those are not statistics. They are the human face of a crisis that Africa has lived with for too long. As Professor Ada Aghaji told a packed hall at the University of Nigeria on October 29, 2026, this is a crisis Africa can no longer afford to ignore. Delivering the institution’s 254th Inaugural Lecture, titled “Let There Be Sight: Building Sustainable Eye Health Systems for All in Africa,” Aghaji, Professor of Ophthalmology and Eye Health Systems, made a simple but very powerful argument: eye health in Africa is not just a medical issue. It is an economic issue. A development issue. A justice issue. And the numbers prove it. According to her, Nigeria loses an estimated $1.6 billion every year in productivity because of vision impairment. Across Africa, the loss is about $9 billion. Globally, it stands at a staggering $410 billion. Behind those figures are livelihoods cut short, schooling interrupted, and families pushed deeper into poverty. Yet, as Aghaji stressed, much of this vision loss can be prevented or treated. A pair of spectacles costing less than a bag of rice. A 15-minute cataract operation. A routine screening at a primary health centre. Why, then, do millions of Africans continue to live with avoidable blindness when the solutions already exist? That was the question at the heart of her lecture. Two Children, Two Worlds Perhaps the most haunting moment of the lecture came not from statistics, but from a story. Aghaji spoke of two children born with congenital rubella syndrome; a condition that can cause cataracts, deafness and other disabilities. One was born in Nigeria. He faced delays, barriers to treatment and rehabilitation, and ended up blind. The other was a Somali refugee child in England. He received timely surgery, spectacles and hearing aids, and with them, a chance to learn, to play, to grow Their medical conditions were similar. Their opportunities were profoundly different. The contrast, Aghaji argued, is the story of Africa’s eye health system in miniature. Medical knowledge alone does not guarantee care. What determines whether a child sees or goes blind is often not the disease, but the system around it: whether there is money to pay, a health worker to detect the problem, a referral that works, a hospital that can be reached. item.title: Naira would’ve been worthless, moved with wheelbarrow if we didn’t act – Tinubu
item.description: President Bola Tinubu said that Naira would have been so worthless, it would be moved about by wheelbarrow if not for his economic policies that moved Nigeria away from the brink of financial collapse. Read Also: Tinubu to Nigerians: ‘I promise better future’ Tinubu, the presidential candidate of All Progressives Congress, APC, said this during his visit to Akwa Ibom State, where he urged voters to support his administration and Governor Umo Eno. He described the January 16, 2027 election as consequential, saying it would determine the country’s direction. Defending his economic policies, Tinubu said his administration had moved Nigeria away from the brink of financial collapse. According to him, “This coming election, on January 16th is a consequential election. It will define the direction of this country. “When I took over, 27 governors out of 36 of this country were unable to pay salary, not to talk of pension, and gratuity. Today, I can say that we are out of that tunnel. “And I can beat my chest to say we are out of the despair, the dark tunnel of uncertainty and the calamity of a possible bankruptcy. “By now if we didn’t take over, if we didn’t do what we did, we will be using the wheelbarrows to move our naira about because it will have become valueless.” On young voters The President urged the electorate, particularly young people, to obtain their Permanent Voter Cards, PVCs. He described it as their most potent instrument for determining the country’s political future. At a reception held in his honour at Ibom Palm Resort, Tinubu praised Eno. He described the resort as evidence of purposeful leadership and the possibility of reclaiming environmentally degraded land for productive use. “We are standing on a resort to the glory of God. It is a product of 73 acres of land of gully erosion, reclaimed, surrounded with a good, romantic, artificial lake, demonstrating a serious vision that is achievable when honest people are working for their homes,” he said. item.title: ADC Crisis: What becomes of Atiku, Mark, Gombe if Supreme Court decides party’s fate?
item.description: By Luminous Jannamike The African Democratic Congress (ADC) was meant to be the meeting point of opposition forces determined to challenge President Bola Tinubu in 2027. Instead, the party has become the battleground for a struggle that could undo the coalition it was expected to accommodate. Read Also: Court sacks Mark-led ADC exco, voids Atiku’s candidacy Barely 24 hours after former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar took his presidential campaign to Sokoto, a Federal High Court judgment delivered by Justice Peter Lifu threw the party into fresh uncertainty, nullifying the David Mark-led leadership and decisions taken under it, including the process that produced Atiku as presidential candidate. For Mark and his allies, it was a setback at a critical moment. For Nafiu Bala Gombe, who challenged the leadership transition, it was a victory in a battle he had refused to abandon. For Atiku, it was a reminder that the platform on which he hopes to return to Aso Rock may not be entirely within his control. With the Mark faction preparing to appeal, attention is shifting to the appellate courts. Whatever the eventual outcome, the political fortunes of some of the coalition’s most prominent figures are at stake. How it all began The dispute began when former ADC National Chairman, Ralph Nwosu, facilitated a leadership transition that brought Mark and former Osun State Governor, Rauf Aregbesola, into the party as National Chairman and National Secretary respectively. The arrangement offered opposition politicians an existing political structure around which to build a challenge to the APC. But Gombe, a former Deputy National Chairman, North, objected, arguing that the party’s constitution provided a succession procedure that was not followed. His challenge produced Justice Lifu’s November 5 judgment. The Mark faction, however, insists that the leadership question had already been examined by the court. It points to the July 2, 2026, judgment of Justice Musa Liman in a separate suit instituted by House of Representatives member Leke Abejide. Justice Liman upheld preliminary objections, including lack of jurisdiction, standing and failure to exhaust internal party remedies. He also made findings favourable to the defendants concerning the leadership transition The Mark camp argues that a court of coordinate jurisdiction cannot overturn another court’s decision. However, the different plaintiffs and the precise issues and reliefs sought in the two cases make the legal relationship between the judgments a matter requiring highest judicial determination. The Supreme Court had intervened on April 30, setting aside an earlier status quo ante bellum order and directing an expedited hearing at the Federal High Court. item.title: ‘Our fathers have spoken’- Middle Belt youths rally behind Tinubu
item.description: Youths from the Middle Belt have declared support for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid, announcing plans to mobilise voters across the region for the All Progressives Congress ahead of the 2027 general elections. The group said it would work with the City Boy Movement, led by Seyi Tinubu, its Director-General, Francis Oluwatosin Shoga, and the APC campaign council to coordinate the mobilisation. The initiative is being championed by aviation entrepreneur and political figure, Isaac Balami, who said the decision followed a meeting between Tinubu and prominent Middle Belt leaders led by elder statesman, General Theophilus Yakubu Danjuma. Balami described the engagement at the Presidential Villa, Abuja, as a turning point for the region, saying younger people were ready to follow the political direction established by their elders. “Our fathers have spoken. They have met the father. We have equally met the son. The movement has begun,” he said. Balami recalled that the same elders had asked him to mobilise support for Labour Party presidential candidate Peter Obi in the 2023 election. He said a fallout over what he described as abandonment had contributed to the latest political realignment. The founder of the National Rebirth Movement, who also serves as an executive board member and National Director on Special Duty of the City Boy Movement, said the decision to support Tinubu was informed by the region’s representation in the administration. He cited appointments to strategic government positions, efforts to tackle insecurity and the inclusion of Middle Belt representatives in national decision-making. “We have people from our region occupying important positions in this government. For us as young people, representation matters,” Balami said. He said the group would mobilise across the Middle Belt, adding that some youths who supported Obi in 2023 were now prepared to back Tinubu. Balami also identified security, infrastructure, education, employment and economic opportunities as issues requiring sustained government attention. He said the movement aimed to involve young people in political decisions affecting the region rather than limit their participation to election campaigns. The announcement follows Thursday’s meeting between Tinubu and a delegation of Middle Belt and North-Central leaders led by Danjuma. The delegation included Defence Minister Christopher Musa, Plateau State Governor Caleb Mutfwang, Taraba State Governor Agbu Kefas, former House of Representatives Speaker Yakubu Dogara and former Chief of Army Staff General Ishaya Bamaiyi. Dogara said the delegation met Tinubu to express solidarity with his administration and discuss security, development and political engagement ahead of the 2027 elections. The emerging youth mobilisation signals an effort to translate the engagement of regional elders into electoral support for Tinubu in an area where Obi secured considerable backing in 2023. item.title: CBN updates guidelines for stablecoins operation
item.description: •Sets N15bn capital requirement By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief The Central Bank of Nigeria has issued guidelines for virtual asset providers in the country, setting minimum capital requirement of N10 billion and N15 billion for Classes 1 and 2 issuers, respectively. This was contained in a circular with reference number PSP/DIR/PUB/CIR/001/004, date November 5, 2026 and signed by the Director of Payments Systems Policy, Mr. Musa Jimoh. According to the bank, “A Class 1 Licensed Issuer shall maintain paid-up capital of N10 billion Naira or such higher amount as the Bank may prescribe, on entry and at all times thereafter. Class 2 Licensed Issuer shall maintain minimum paid-up capital of N15 billion or such higher amount as the Bank may prescribe, on entry and at all times thereafter. “Both classes shall comply with the capital deposit and corresponding evidence and supplementary requirements in Section 17. There is no offshore issuer exemption from incorporation, licensing or capital.” Class 2 stablecoins are digital tokens designed to maintain a stable value against foreign currencies, including the US dollar, while Class 1 refers to issuers of naira-referenced stablecoins. CBN said the emergence of virtual assets, stablecoins, and tokenised payment instruments “presents significant opportunities for innovation in payments, remittances, settlement, and digital commerce,” but that, “their growing adoption also introduces risks relating to financial stability, monetary policy, consumer protection, illicit finance, operational resilience, and foreign exchange management.” It added that the guidelines were issued pursuant to its statutory mandate to promote monetary and financial stability and regulate Nigeria’s payments system. “These Guidelines establish a risk-based framework for the licensing, regulation, supervision, and oversight of Non-Security Virtual Assets, including stablecoins, Deposit Money Tokens (DMTs), and related Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs). “These Guidelines seek to support responsible innovation while safeguarding the integrity, stability, and efficiency of the Nigerian financial system. “These Guidelines also seek to provide regulatory requirements relating to governance, prudential standards, consumer protection, operational resilience, AML/CFT/CPF compliance, and reporting obligations for entities and persons engaged in regulated non-security virtual asset activities within or involving Nigeria,” the bank explained. The CBN’s updated framework outlines clear boundaries for Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs), with a sharp focus on foreign exchange liquidity, consumer protection, and peer-to-peer (P2P) trading identity protocols. Curbing money laundering The guidelines place great responsibilities on issuers to ensure that their activities do not aid money laundering or terrorism financing, as they are required to provide detailed data on their customers. item.title: Ebonyi Youths Protest Political Violence, Intimidation Ahead Of 2027 Elections
item.description: Hundreds of youths in Ebonyi State have staged a peaceful march through Abakaliki, the state capital, calling for an end to political violence, intimidation and harassment of opposition members ahead of the 2027 general elections. The protesters, under the aegis of Concerned Ebonyi Youth for Democracy, said they came from the 13 local government areas of the state to demand a peaceful political atmosphere in which all citizens can participate without fear. The demonstrators marched through major streets in Abakaliki, displaying placards with messages including, “Democracy Needs Peaceful Ideas, Not Weapons” and “Protect Freedom of Speech in Ebonyi.” Addressing journalists during the rally, a spokesperson for the group said the youths would not accept any attempt to undermine their constitutional rights. “Our constitutional rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly are not negotiable,” the spokesperson said. The group also expressed concern over reported incidents of physical violence, harassment and voter intimidation targeting opposition figures in parts of the state. “We will not sit by while political thuggery and intimidation threaten to ruin our state’s democratic process. Every citizen, regardless of party alignment, deserves to participate without fear for their safety,” the spokesperson added. The protesters called on security agencies and state institutions to intervene and ensure a level playing field for all political parties. Another youth coordinator said opposition parties should be able to campaign, present their programmes and engage voters without threats or intimidation. “Opposition parties must be allowed to campaign safely, present their platforms, and engage with voters without constant threat of violence,” the coordinator said. The group said the march was part of efforts by young people in the state to demand accountability and promote peaceful political participation as the 2027 general elections approach.
